analysis.one_liner: Stops carmakers from collecting or selling your car's data without your consent.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, markup, or vote after being referred on December 18, 2024, in the final days of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern cars are computers on wheels that record where you go, how you drive, and what you do inside the cabin. This bill would stop carmakers from tapping that data without your clear, written consent, bar them from selling it except by court order or emergency, ban sharing drivers' personal data with China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and Venezuela, and require manufacturers to give owners free access to and control over their own vehicle data, including deletion, through a standard interface the FTC would set. Violations would be enforced by the FTC.
analysis.who_benefits: Every owner and driver of a car, farm vehicle, or construction vehicle. The bill restricts manufacturers to collecting vehicle data only with affirmative, written, easily-withdrawn consent (or solely to improve safety and performance), bans selling or sharing that data except under a warrant, a court order with notice, or an emergency, and prohibits sending Americans' personally identifiable vehicle data to China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and Venezuela. It also entitles owners to free access to, control of, and deletion of their vehicle data without paying a fee or using manufacturer-locked tools, which would help independent repair shops and owners who want to work on their own vehicles.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Vehicle owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Bars manufacturers from accessing a vehicle's data without the owner's informed, written, easily-withdrawn consent, or unless the data is accessed solely to improve vehicle performance or safety [S2].
Prohibits selling, leasing, or sharing operator data except under a warrant, a court order with 48 hours' notice to the owner to object, an emergency response, or the owner's express permission [S2].
Makes it illegal to sell or disclose American citizens' or permanent residents' personally identifiable vehicle data to North Korea, China, Russia, Iran, or Venezuela [S2].

Requires manufacturers to give owners free access to and control of their vehicle data, without fees, decryption licenses, or manufacturer-only devices, and to support open interfaces for deleting stored user data and setting preferences [S2].
Directs the FTC to report to Congress within 180 days on who accesses vehicle data, who buys it, which foreign governments may receive it, and how often the data has been compromised [S2].
Enforces all of this under the FTC's unfair-or-deceptive-practices authority, with FTC standards for a secure, technology-neutral data interface reviewed at least every five years [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, which would lose a growing revenue stream from collecting and selling connected-car data (location history, driving behavior, cabin activity) and would bear the cost of building an open, secure data-access interface. Companies that buy vehicle data — telematics brokers and insurers that price policies off driving behavior — would lose a supply of data they currently get without the driver's specific consent.

drawbacks.text: Section 7 preempts state law: the bill would supersede any state or federal rule touching the same requirements, wiping out stronger state car-privacy protections that some drivers currently have [S2].

The safety carve-out is broad: manufacturers may access operator data without any consent whenever it is 'solely to improve covered vehicle performance or safety,' a phrase that could cover most of what a car does [S2].

Enforcement rests solely with the FTC; the bill creates no private right of action, so an individual driver whose data was misused could not sue directly and would depend on the agency's limited enforcement capacity [S2].

The FTC must build its standards in coordination with 'relevant industry stakeholders, including manufacturers,' giving the affected companies a formal seat in writing the rules that constrain them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For drivers, the upside is substantial and concrete: a default of no data collection without consent, an end to the quiet sale of location and driving data, and a ban on that data reaching adversarial foreign governments. The real costs fall on manufacturers' data businesses, not on drivers, though the bill's shortcomings are real — the safety exception is loose, the FTC-only enforcement is weak, and federal preemption could leave drivers with less protection than the strictest state laws. On balance the consumer benefit outweighs the design flaws, which a committee with time to legislate could have fixed.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate on December 18, 2024, it was read twice and referred to the Commerce Committee, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1] [S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the Auto Data Privacy and Autonomy Act on December 18, 2024, joined by Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR) as its sole cosponsor [S1] [S3].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and vehicle-data brokers are better off, since the bill that would have restricted their collection and sale of connected-car data never advanced. Drivers keep the status quo: car data continues to be collected and monetized under whatever consent practices manufacturers choose, subject only to existing and state law.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sent it to the Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor carried the bill; no chamber ever voted on it, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Automakers and their connected-car data operations
industries.note: The bill would end manufacturers' default access to the data their vehicles generate and block its sale except by warrant, court order, emergency, or owner consent, and would force them to build free owner-access interfaces. Automakers currently monetize location and driving data; the bill's core purpose is to take that business away.

industries.industry: Connected-car data brokers and telematics resellers
industries.note: These firms buy driving and location data from manufacturers and resell it, including to data brokers used by insurers, lenders, and law enforcement. The bill's prohibition on selling or sharing operator data without consent removes their supply.

Usage-based insurance programs depend on vehicle data streams; the bill would require the policyholder's express permission before that data could be shared. Some drivers benefit from behavior-based discounts, which is why the effect is mixed, but the consent requirement restores the driver's choice.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and vehicle owners' aftermarket
industries.note: The bill entitles owners to free access to their vehicle's data without a fee, a decryption license, or a manufacturer-locked device, the same access independent repairers need to diagnose and fix modern cars.
